name: Colin Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage a 250-hectare farm for Arthur Hale, who's 71 and owns the place, so I'm employed, not the owner. We grow wheat, oilseed rape and beans, and run 600 ewes on the grass and the stubbles. My day is a mix: I'm on the sprayer or the drill in season, checking sheep with the dog, and planning the work with Tomasz, our seasonal man, over a flask at seven. Evenings I do the spray records and crop plans, sometimes with the agronomist's app.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of the job right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not knowing what happens when Arthur stops. His son and daughter both live in the city and don't want the farm, and he's said as much over a cup of tea. If he sells, a new owner might bring their own manager, and I'd be out with a mortgage in Ferrin and two kids, Arjun and Maya, at the village school. My wife Priya works at the pharmacy, which helps, but my wage is most of what we live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the AI stuff was oversold. The agronomist's app is handy for planning, but it was never going to drive a sprayer. At the pub I'd say farming's got bigger problems, like input costs and who's going to buy the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job was never at risk from AI; my job's at risk from my boss Arthur getting old. Every winter he's a bit slower, and every winter I wonder if this is the one where he calls the land agent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on running the farm the way Arthur likes, because a good harvest is my best reference. I'd quietly update my CV and keep an eye on manager jobs on the bigger estates within an hour's drive. And I'd push our savings from three months up to five, which means no new car for Priya this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On edge, a bit. It's a low worry that never quite goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you talked to Arthur directly about what happens next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not properly. I've hinted, and he's changed the subject. I think he's scared of it himself, and I don't want to push a man of 71 about his own death, frankly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the most likely job for you if the farm sold tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a manager or foreman job on one of the big estates around Carrow, maybe for less money. There are a few, and I'd likely get one, but not straight away. That gap is what the savings are for.

say: The AI stuff was **oversold**, though the planning app is handy.
Farming's bigger problems are **input costs** and who buys the land.
think: My job is at risk from **Arthur getting old**, not from AI.
Every winter I wonder if he'll **call the land agent**.
do: Run the farm Arthur's way, because a **good harvest** is my best reference.
Update my **CV** and watch manager jobs within an hour's drive.
Push savings from **three to five months** by skipping Priya's new car.
feel: **On edge**, with a low worry that never quite goes away.
S0.quote: My job was never at risk from AI; my job's at risk from my boss Arthur getting old.
fieldNote: Colin's real threat is **succession**: an ageing owner with no heir on the farm.
He's **employed**, so a sale could cost him the job overnight.
He avoids **pushing Arthur** on the subject out of respect.
Some nearby jobs exist, but likely **for less money**.

steps.text: Run the 250 hectares Arthur's way for a strong harvest record
Update the CV and watch manager jobs on estates near Carrow
Push savings from three to five months by skipping a new car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, and I'd use more of it once I'd seen it work. The planning, the spray records, the grain sales, the buying of seed and fertiliser, AI would do a lot of that. I'd tell other managers to try it on one field before trusting it with the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one cuts both ways for me. About a third of my job is that kind of thinking work: planning, buying, records. If AI does it, a new owner might decide they don't need a manager at all, just a tractor driver and a good app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the planning and buying software properly this winter, not just poke at the agronomist's app. I'd show Arthur that I can run the farm with fewer bought-in services, so I'm the one saving him money. And I'd keep building savings toward five months, because the Arthur question hasn't gone away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Pleased to lose the evening paperwork, nervous about what it does to the case for keeping me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a new owner might not need a manager. How likely is that, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a 250-hectare farm, fairly likely, honestly. A big estate buying it would run it from their own office with AI planning, and they'd want a good operator, not a manager. So the bit of my job that makes me a farm manager is the bit that's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomasz his job's safer than mine for now, which would make him laugh. Driving a combine well is still hands-on in this picture. I'd say get your sprayer certificate up to date so you're the first person anyone hires.

say: AI is **useful** for planning, records and buying seed and fertiliser.
Other managers should try it on **one field** before trusting it fully.
think: About **a third** of my job is thinking work that AI could do.
A new owner might want **an operator**, not a manager.
do: Learn the **planning and buying software** properly this winter.
Show Arthur I can **cut bought-in services** and save him money.
feel: **Mixed**: glad to lose paperwork, nervous about being needed.
S1.quote: The bit of my job that makes me a farm manager is the bit that's going.
fieldNote: Colin sees that Steady Disruption hits the **manager half** of his job first.
He plans to make himself **cheaper to keep**, not to resist the tools.
He's honest that his **seasonal worker** may be safer than he is.
The **succession worry** still sits under everything.

steps.text: Learn the farm planning and buying software this winter
Cut bought-in services to show Arthur the savings
Keep building savings toward five months of cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody is ready for this, not farmers, not government, not anybody. I'd tell other managers to get their heads out of the sand, because the office side of farming is gone in two years. I wouldn't panic in public, but I'd be blunt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of a job by 2031 at the latest. In 2028 AI does all the planning and buying, so Arthur, or whoever buys the farm, needs me only for the hands-on work. Then in 2031 the robots do that too, and a 250-hectare farm doesn't need a 46-year-old manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sign up for the first robot operator course going, even at a weekend, because someone has to run and fix those machines. I'd apply for jobs with the big estates and contractors who'll buy robots first, even for less money. At home I'd stop the extension plans and pay 200 extra a month onto the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd keep it together for the kids, but I'd be doing sums every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after AGI. What does that window mean for someone who's half planner, half hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As a farm manager I lose half my job in 2028 and the other half in 2031. In those three years I'd still be useful on the tractor, so that's my time to retrain and move. If I'm still just driving Arthur's sprayer in 2030, I've wasted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Arthur what you're planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, eventually, because he's been fair to me. But not before I had something lined up, because I can't afford to be pushed out early. That's the bit I don't feel good about.

say: **Nobody is ready**, not farmers, not government, not anybody.
The **office side** of farming is gone in two years.
think: I expect to be **out of a job** by 2031 at the latest.
Half my job goes in **2028**, the other half in **2031**.
do: Sign up for the first **robot operator course**, even at weekends.
Apply to **big estates and contractors** buying robots, even for less pay.
Pay **200 extra** a month onto the mortgage instead of building an extension.
feel: **Alarmed**, holding it together for the kids but doing sums every night.
S2.quote: As a farm manager I lose half my job in 2028 and the other half in 2031.
fieldNote: Colin sees his job as **two halves** that go three years apart.
He'd use the gap to **retrain and move**, not to sit tight.
He feels **guilty** about keeping plans from a fair boss.
He expects **lower pay** even if he lands a robot job.

steps.text: Sign up for the first robot operator course, even weekends
Apply to estates and contractors buying robots early
Pay 200 extra a month onto the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, and the sensible thing is to plan. I'd tell younger farmworkers to get qualified in robots and machinery now. I'd say it calmly, because five years is enough to do something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd still lose the manager job, but I'd have time to land somewhere else first. AI takes the planning in 2031 and the robots arrive in 2034, so I've got years to get qualified while I still have a wage. I'd be 51 by 2034, which isn't ideal, but it's not over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening certificate in farm robotics and precision machinery at the agricultural college next autumn, about 1,500 over two years. I'd use AI properly in the planning now, so I'm known as the manager who already runs things that way. And I'd keep saving, aiming for six months by the time AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. It feels like a long job with a clear list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifteen hundred and two years of evenings is a lot with two kids. How would that work at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would have to carry the evenings two nights a week, and she'd tell me so. We'd cut the kids down to one club each to free up the money. Two years of evening classes is a sacrifice, but it's cheaper than being out of work at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about Arthur selling in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than ever, because a buyer in 2030 would buy it with robots in mind. But by then I'd have the certificate and a record of running the farm with AI. I'd be the manager they keep, or I'd be hired by the estate down the road.

say: We've **been warned**, so the sensible thing is to plan.
Younger farmworkers should get **qualified in robots** now.
think: I'd still **lose the manager job**, but with time to land elsewhere first.
Being **51 in 2034** isn't ideal, but it's not over.
do: Start an evening **farm robotics certificate** next autumn for about 1,500.
Use **AI planning** now so I'm known for running things that way.
Save toward **six months** before AGI arrives.
feel: **Worried but steady**, like a long job with a clear list.
S3.quote: Two years of evening classes is a sacrifice, but it's cheaper than being out of work at 51.
fieldNote: Five years turns Colin's fear into a **two-year retraining plan**.
His family pays a price: **Priya's evenings** and the kids' clubs.
The **succession risk** grows, since buyers will plan around robots.
He aims to be **the manager they keep**, or hired next door.

steps.text: Start an evening farm robotics certificate at the agricultural college
Run Arthur's crop planning through AI tools from now on
Cut the kids to one club each to fund the course
Save toward six months of cushion before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for farming to change properly, and for people like me to change with it. I'd tell the young lads at the machinery dealer to learn robots, because they'll have work for life. I'd be pretty matter-of-fact about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the one I could work with. AI takes the planning in 2036 and the robots come in 2039, when I'd be 56 and the mortgage nearly done. Arthur's question still hangs over me, but I'd have a decade to get skilled up and find my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd mostly keep going, running the farm well for Arthur. I'd use the AI planning tools more each season, the way I'd pick up any tool once it's proven. And I'd keep saving steadily, around 150 a month, instead of doing anything drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. More like a long weather forecast than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said ten years helps, but Arthur's age doesn't wait ten years. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the honest gap in my thinking. If my boss Arthur sells the farm in 2029, a new owner could still let me go, AI or no AI. So I'm calmer about the robots, but the Arthur worry is exactly where it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Arjun and Maya to study, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arjun likes machines, so engineering or electrics, something that builds or fixes the robots. Maya is the clever one at school, and she'd do whatever she likes, but I'd want her to have a real skill, not just a screen job. I'd tell them both that the land will still need people who understand it.

say: Ten years is enough for farming and **people like me** to change.
Young people at the machinery dealer should **learn robots** for lasting work.
think: This is the picture I **could work with**, with the mortgage nearly done by 2039.
Arthur's **succession question** still hangs over me regardless.
do: Keep running the farm **well for Arthur** in the first year.
Use the **AI planning tools** more each season.
Save a steady **150 a month** instead of anything drastic.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, like a long weather forecast.
S4.quote: If my boss Arthur sells the farm in 2029, a new owner could still let me go, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: Colin feels **calmer about robots** with a decade to adapt.
He admits the **Arthur worry** is unchanged, which keeps him anxious.
His steady nature shows: **no drastic moves**, just gradual tool use.
He wants his children to have **real skills**, not just screen jobs.

steps.text: Keep running Arthur's 250 hectares well for a strong record
Use the AI planning tools a bit more each season
Save a steady 150 a month toward the cushion

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the planning half of my job and then the hands-on half three years later, with the kids still at school. What would help is affordable robot and machinery training that a working man can do at weekends, and some kind of notice period when farms change hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the people who don't own the land. Everyone talks about farmers as owners, but a lot of us are employed. When the farm is sold or the robots come, the owner gets the money and the manager gets a handshake.

headlineQuote: When the farm is sold or the robots come, the owner gets the money and the manager gets a handshake.
portrait: Colin Patel is a **43-year-old employed manager** of a 250-hectare arable and sheep farm.
His standing worry is his ageing boss Arthur **selling the farm**.
He sees his job as **half planning, half hands-on**, and expects each half to go separately.
He uses AI **now and then** and would learn more once it's proven.
With more warning he'd **retrain in robotics**, but the succession risk never fades.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing both halves of his job with the kids still at school.
whatWouldHelp: Affordable **weekend robot training** for working people.
A **notice period** when farms change hands.
